questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. A step with no record, tested once or routinely
questions.question: A pharmacy requires a second pharmacist to witness each opening of the controlled-drug safe. The keypad logs each opening under the opener's code. Which method best lets an internal auditor test whether witnessing routinely happens?

options.A: Walk through one safe opening with the pharmacist on duty.
options.B: Interview the pharmacists who open the safe on each shift.
options.C: Observe openings at unannounced times over several shifts.
options.D: Inspect the keypad log of every safe opening across the year.

questions.key_concept: When no record captures a step, observation is the source, and showing it is routine takes repeated observation, not one walk-through.
questions.pre_read: Does the question ask whether the step can be done, or whether it is done routinely? Which source could show each?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 requires information that is relevant and sufficient, and its considerations list directly observing a process as one way to gather it. The keypad log does not record the witness, so observation is the source, and watching openings at unannounced times on several shifts shows whether witnessing is routine. One walk-through, the closest choice, shows the step done once, which cannot show a routine.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a walk-through is a direct observation, but one opening shows only that the step can be done. It cannot show that witnessing happens routinely.
wrong_explanations.B: Interviews show what pharmacists say they do. Statements from the people performing the step need corroboration and cannot show by themselves that witnessing happens.
wrong_explanations.D: The keypad log covers every opening in the year, but it records the code that opened the safe, not who witnessed it, so it cannot answer this objective.

tips: Eliminate: B, because pharmacists' own statements need corroboration before they show practice, and D, because the keypad log covers the year but does not record the witness.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.1 asks for sufficient information; one walk-through shows the step once, while unannounced observation on several shifts shows whether it is routine.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, one walk-through shows how a step works. Whether it happens routinely needs repeated observation, or records that capture the step, across the period.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. An objective about what staff know
questions.question: An engagement at a mining firm's 60 sites asks whether site staff know how to raise a safety incident under the new policy. Which source best serves the internal auditor?

options.A: A questionnaire asking sampled staff to describe the steps.
options.B: The incident log, showing how many reports each site filed.
options.C: Site managers' signed checklists confirming staff were briefed.
options.D: The approved policy and the training plan that rolled it out.

questions.key_concept: Relevance comes from the objective: when the question is what staff know, asking staff to show that knowledge is direct evidence of the condition.
questions.pre_read: What exactly does the objective ask about: what was done, what was planned, or what people know?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 makes information relevant when it fits the engagement objective, and its considerations list surveying the people involved. Here the condition is what staff know, so asking sampled staff to describe the steps, and checking each answer against the policy, tests that knowledge directly. Managers' signed checklists, the closest choice, show that briefings were held, not that the people briefed know the route.

wrong_explanations.B: A count of reports filed shows activity, not knowledge. A site with few reports may simply have had few incidents, so the log cannot show what staff know.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the checklists show that briefings happened, as the managers report them. Being briefed is not the same as knowing, and the objective asks about knowledge.
wrong_explanations.D: The policy and training plan describe what should happen. They are the criteria, not evidence of what staff at the 60 sites actually know.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a count of reports shows how often incidents were filed, not whether staff know how, and D, because the policy and plan state the criteria.
Final two: A beats C because the objective is staff knowledge; a questionnaire that asks staff to describe the steps tests it directly, while a checklist records only that a briefing took place.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, let the objective pick the source. When the condition is what people know or believe, asking them is direct evidence, not a weak substitute.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. A whole population from an editable file
questions.question: A county government's procurement head emails an internal auditor a spreadsheet of all 4,200 purchase orders. The head's team maintains it. The auditor finds an approval recorded in every row. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Enough to conclude: every order was tested, not a sample.
options.B: Enough to conclude once totals match the team's monthly reports.
options.C: Not enough yet: suppliers should confirm each order's delivery.
options.D: Not enough yet: the file comes from the team under review.

questions.key_concept: A full-population test is only as good as its data: a file kept by the team under review is checked against the source first.
questions.pre_read: Before counting how much was tested, ask who produced the data and whether it could have been changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 says reliability is strengthened when the internal auditor obtains information directly, or from a system with effective controls, and Standard 4.3 requires critically assessing reliability. A spreadsheet maintained by the team under review is neither, so testing all 4,200 rows adds coverage, not trust. Whole-population testing, the closest choice, is only as good as its data: the auditor should take the orders from the purchasing system directly before concluding.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: testing every row removes sampling risk, but not the risk that the rows were altered. Volume never makes up for information that is not yet reliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Both documents come from the same team, so agreement between them is not independent corroboration. A file and reports from one source can match and both be wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Delivery confirmations bear on whether goods arrived, not on whether orders were approved. They come from an outside party, but they do not fit this objective.

tips: Eliminate: B, because two records from the same team do not corroborate each other independently, and C, because delivery evidence does not answer whether orders were approved.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.1 ties reliability to who obtained the data and the system behind it; testing every row of the team's own spreadsheet tests the file, not the orders.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a full-population test inherits the quality of its data. Ask who produced the file and whether it could be changed before trusting the count.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. A first-hand extract from a weakly controlled system
questions.question: An internal auditor queried a hospital's pharmacy stock system directly. A review last month found that staff can overwrite quantities with no log or review. Which view of the query results is most accurate?

options.A: Strong: the auditor obtained the quantities first-hand from the system.
options.B: Weakened: the system behind them lacks effective controls.
options.C: Weakened: the data came from the activity's own system.
options.D: Strong: the figures are current and come from the official record.

questions.key_concept: Reliability has three separate factors; getting data first-hand does not repair figures held in a system whose controls over changes are missing.
questions.pre_read: Check each reliability factor on its own: who obtained the data, what corroborates it, and how well controlled its source system is.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 names three things that strengthen reliability: the internal auditor obtaining information directly or from an independent source, corroboration, and a system with effective governance, risk management and control processes. The auditor's first-hand query meets the first, but quantities anyone can overwrite unseen fail the third, so the figures need corroboration, such as a count, before use. First-hand retrieval, the closest choice, cannot repair weak data at its source.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: obtaining data directly does strengthen reliability, but only for how it was retrieved. Quantities that staff can change unseen may be wrong before the auditor's query runs.
wrong_explanations.C: Querying the activity's own system is normal. The auditor obtained the data directly, which meets the first factor; the weakness is the missing control over changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Current, official figures are reliable only when the system that holds them is well controlled. Here last month's review found the controls over changes missing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a direct query of the activity's own system meets the first reliability factor, and D, because official figures are only as good as the controls over them.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.1 counts the system behind the data as its own reliability factor; retrieving it first-hand does not fix figures anyone can overwrite.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, test all three reliability factors separately: who obtained it, what corroborates it, and how well controlled its source system is.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. A sample the activity selected
questions.question: An internal auditor tested 25 of a retailer's 610 vendor master changes. The methodology sets that sample size. The vendor team lead selected the 25, and all were authorized. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Too weak for the 610: the audited unit, not the auditor, chose them.
options.B: Too weak for the 610: 25 items cannot represent so many changes.
options.C: Enough for the 610: each tested change carried the required approval.
options.D: Enough for the 610: another auditor could repeat the 25 tests.

questions.key_concept: Sufficient means a competent reviewer would reach the same conclusion about the whole population, which a sample the audited team chose may not represent.
questions.pre_read: Ask what population the conclusion covers, and whether the items tested were chosen so that they stand for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.1, evidence is sufficient when someone careful, informed and capable could redo the work program and arrive at the same conclusions, and its considerations say a sample should be as representative of the population as possible. Items the audited team picked may leave out the changes that matter. Repeating the 25 tests, the closest choice, would only confirm those 25; it says nothing yet about the other 585.

wrong_explanations.B: The methodology sets 25 for this population, so size is not the gap. A sample of that size can support a conclusion when it is chosen to represent all changes.
wrong_explanations.C: The tests show those 25 were authorized. A clean result speaks for all 610 only if the sample represents them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: repeatability is part of the test, but the reviewer must also reach the same conclusion about all 610. Redoing a hand-picked sample does not get there.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the methodology already sets 25 for this population, and C, because a clean result on 25 items speaks for all 610 only if they represent the rest.
Final two: A beats D because Standard 14.1's reviewer must reach the same conclusion, not just the same 25 results; a sample the audited team chose may not represent the year.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about sufficiency, ask who chose the items and what population they stand for. A sample supports only what it represents.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. A walk-through that contradicts the approved map
questions.question: At a retailer, management's approved map shows a supervisor approving every credit note. An internal auditor's walk-through of three credit notes found none approved. What is the best basis for the condition?

options.A: The approved map, treating the three credit notes as exceptions.
options.B: How the three credit notes were handled when followed through.
options.C: The process the billing clerks describe when interviewed.
options.D: The billing policy on which credit notes need approval.

questions.key_concept: The condition is what evidence shows the process does; a map, however approved, shows the design management intends.
questions.pre_read: Which of these shows how the process is meant to run, and which shows how it actually runs?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 requires the condition to be determined from information and evidence gathered during the engagement. Following real credit notes through the process is first-hand evidence of how it runs, so the observed practice is the condition. The approved map, the closest choice, shows how management says the process should run; calling three unapproved notes exceptions assumes a result the testing has not shown.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an approved map shows the intended design, which can inform the criteria. Three walk-throughs that all contradict it are evidence about the condition, not exceptions to set aside.
wrong_explanations.C: What clerks describe is a statement that needs corroboration. The walk-through has already shown the real practice, so the clerks' account cannot override it.
wrong_explanations.D: The policy says which notes need approval, which makes it criteria. The condition is what actually happens, and that comes from evidence.

tips: Eliminate: C, because interview statements need corroboration and cannot outweigh what was observed, and D, because a policy sets the criteria, not the condition.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.2 sets the condition from evidence gathered; an approved map is management's design, and three contrary walk-throughs are evidence, not exceptions.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a process map is a claim about design until real items are walked through it. Condition comes from evidence; criteria from what should be.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. Entries flagged by anomaly detection
questions.question: Anomaly detection on a manufacturer's 90,000 journal entries flags 160 as out of pattern, such as weekend postings. Which next step is best for the internal auditor?

options.A: Log the 160 as potential findings, then ask staff to explain each.
options.B: Ask the controller to reverse the 160 entries before closing.
options.C: Run the same detection on last year's entries for comparison.
options.D: Check each of the 160 against the posting policy and its support.

questions.key_concept: An analytics flag shows an entry is unusual; it becomes a potential finding only when evidence shows it differs from the criteria.
questions.pre_read: Is an unusual entry the same thing as an entry that breaks a rule?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.2, a potential finding is a gap between what the criteria require and the condition the evidence shows. An entry flagged as unusual has broken a pattern, not yet a rule: a weekend posting may be allowed. Checking each against the posting policy and its support shows which ones differ from the criteria. Logging all 160 as potential findings first, the closest choice, treats the tool's pattern as the criteria.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: following up is right, but labeling all 160 as potential findings first treats unusual as wrong. Only a difference from the criteria makes a potential finding.
wrong_explanations.B: Correcting entries is management's decision, and only once an entry is shown to be wrong. Reversing entries no one has examined could undo valid postings.
wrong_explanations.C: A second year's flags would show whether the pattern is new, which can help later. It cannot show whether any of these 160 entries breaks the posting policy.

tips: Eliminate: B, because correcting entries is management's call once an error is shown, and C, because another year's flags say nothing about whether these 160 break the policy.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.2 makes a potential finding a difference from the criteria; a flag only shows an entry is unusual until it is checked against the rule.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, an analytics flag is a lead. It becomes a potential finding only when evidence shows the condition differs from the criteria.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. An answer held in unstructured contract text
questions.question: An internal auditor must learn whether a mining company's supplier contracts contain an anti-bribery clause. Each contract is stored as a text file, with separate fields for dates, values and parties. Which analysis best fits?

options.A: Query the system's structured fields, which cover every contract.
options.B: Read 30 contract files from the largest unit, clause by clause.
options.C: Search every contract file for the clause's key wording.
options.D: Ask each contract owner to confirm the clause is included.

questions.key_concept: Find where the answer is recorded before choosing the method: when it sits in free text, text analysis of the unstructured data fits.
questions.pre_read: Which data source could actually show whether a contract contains the clause?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 requires information consistent with the engagement objective. The question is what each contract says, and the fields hold only dates, values and parties, so the answer sits in the contract files: unstructured data that text analysis can search for the clause's wording across every contract. Querying the structured fields, the closest choice, uses complete, tidy data that cannot show whether the clause is there.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the structured fields cover every contract, but none records the clause. Complete data that does not hold the answer is not relevant to this objective.
wrong_explanations.B: Reading contracts is the right source, but 30 from one unit cannot speak for every contract. A search of every file covers the whole population at little cost.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners' confirmations are statements from the people responsible for the contracts. The contracts themselves are on file, so the auditor can examine them first-hand.

tips: Eliminate: B, because 30 contracts from one unit do not represent all contracts, and D, because owners' confirmations are statements when the contracts can be examined first-hand.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.1 asks for information that fits the objective; the fields cover every contract but hold nothing about the clause, which sits in the contract files.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, find where the answer is recorded before picking the method. Free text is unstructured data, and text analysis is how to read it at scale.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. An independent headcount for the expectation
questions.question: A retailer's payroll cost rose 12%. An internal auditor builds an expectation for it from the pay raise and average headcount. HR keeps staff records separately from payroll. Which headcount source best serves the test?

options.A: The payroll system's count, as it covers the people being paid.
options.B: Last year's count plus planned hires, as the budget used them.
options.C: The payroll manager's estimate, as the manager knows the staff.
options.D: The HR records' count, as HR records each hire and leaver.

questions.key_concept: An analytical expectation needs drivers from a source independent of the figure tested; a payroll headcount rises with any false employees.
questions.pre_read: If someone added false employees to payroll, which headcount would rise with the cost, and which would not?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2's considerations include relating payroll expense to the average number of employees, and Standard 14.1 says information is more reliable when it comes from an independent source or is corroborated. HR records kept apart from payroll can expose a cost rise that headcount does not explain. The payroll system's own count, the closest choice, would rise with any false employees added to payroll, so the expectation would hide the gap it should reveal.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the payroll count does cover the people paid, which is the problem: any false employee added to payroll raises cost and count together, so the gap disappears.
wrong_explanations.B: Planned hires show what the budget expected, not who was actually employed. An expectation built on them tests payroll against the plan, not against reality.
wrong_explanations.C: An estimate from the manager responsible for payroll is a statement from the activity under review. It is neither independent nor a record of who was employed.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the payroll manager's estimate is a statement from the activity under review, and B, because planned hires show the budget, not who was actually employed.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.1 favors information from an independent source; a headcount drawn from payroll itself moves with the cost it is meant to test.
Exam cue: on CIA analytical review questions, take the drivers of an expectation from a source independent of the figure being tested, or the comparison can hide the problem.

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. Stating the effect when no loss has occurred
questions.question: At a lender, an internal auditor finds that 14 loan officers can change borrowers' bank details without review. Tests found no misuse this year. Which of the following best states the finding's effect?

options.A: Payouts could be redirected to accounts that no one has checked.
options.B: None so far, since tests found no misuse during the year.
options.C: The breach of the policy requiring review of detail changes.
options.D: The cost management could incur to add a review step.

questions.key_concept: A finding's effect is the potential exposure the gap creates; it exists while the gap is open, whether or not a loss has happened.
questions.pre_read: Keep the parts of a finding apart: criteria, condition, root cause and effect. Which one is each option describing?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires internal auditors to determine the potential effects of each potential finding, and its considerations describe the effect as the risk or potential exposure, often estimated with input from management. Payouts that could go to accounts no one checks are that exposure, whether or not misuse has happened yet. No effect, the closest choice, confuses what has happened with what could happen.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: no misuse found is good news, but the effect is the potential exposure. A gap that could let payouts be redirected matters before any loss occurs.
wrong_explanations.C: Unreviewed changes measured against the policy are the condition and the criteria of the finding. The effect is what that gap could cause.
wrong_explanations.D: The cost of a fix matters when weighing recommendations or action plans. It is not the effect of the gap.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the gap between policy and practice is the condition against the criteria, and D, because the cost of a fix belongs to weighing the action, not the effect.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 14.3 asks for potential effects; an exposure exists while the gap is open, whether or not a loss has occurred yet.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, keep the parts of a finding apart: criteria (what should be), condition (what is), root cause (why) and effect (what could result).

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. Ranking findings with the function's methodology
questions.question: An internal auditor finds the function's rating scale too coarse for an engagement at a port. The port's manager asks that findings be ranked by cost to fix. How should the auditor best rank them?

options.A: By the cost to fix, as the port's manager requests.
options.B: By the money at stake, the measure the board reads most easily.
options.C: On a finer scale fitted to this engagement, explained in the report.
options.D: On the existing scale, with the concern raised separately.

questions.key_concept: Findings are ranked with the chief audit executive's methodology so ratings stay consistent across engagements; a better method is proposed, not used alone.
questions.pre_read: Who sets the method for rating findings, and what would a different scale do to comparisons with other engagements?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires each finding to be ranked by significance with the chief audit executive's methodology, and its considerations say this keeps ratings consistent across engagements. The auditor rates on the function's scale and takes the view that it is too coarse to the chief audit executive, who owns the method. A scale fitted to this engagement, the closest choice, sounds careful but makes these ratings mean something different from every other engagement's.

wrong_explanations.A: Cost to fix can help management order its action plans. Significance rests on likelihood and impact, so the manager's preference does not set the ranking.
wrong_explanations.B: Money is one part of impact. Significance also weighs likelihood and other factors, so ranking by money alone can misrank a small but serious gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a finer scale may describe this engagement better, but Standard 14.3 requires the chief audit executive's methodology. A private scale breaks consistency across engagements.

tips: Eliminate: A, because significance rests on likelihood and impact rather than the cost of a fix, and B, because money alone leaves out likelihood and the nature of the risk.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 14.3 requires prioritizing with the chief audit executive's methodology; a better scale is proposed to the chief audit executive, not used alone.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the internal auditor applies the function's methodology and proposes changes to it; changing it alone for one engagement is the trap.

questions.subtopic: 2B7 Workpapers that support the results. A workpaper with no population or selection
questions.question: An internal auditor's workpaper covers claim payments at an insurer. It lists the 60 claims tested, what was checked on each, the 4 exceptions and the auditor's initials. What does it most need before review?

options.A: The claims manager's sign-off on the 4 exceptions.
options.B: The population and the method used to pick the sample.
options.C: The engagement risk assessment behind this test.
options.D: A cross-reference to the work program step this test completes.

questions.key_concept: A complete workpaper lets another competent auditor repeat the test, which needs the population and how items were selected, not only the results.
questions.pre_read: Could another auditor redo this test from the file alone, and if not, what is missing?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 requires work to be documented well enough that another informed, careful internal auditor could redo it and get the same results, and its considerations list the population, sample size and selection method in a workpaper's basic format. Without them, no one could repeat the selection. A cross-reference to the work program, the closest choice, points to the planned approach, not the population actually tested or how the sample was drawn.

wrong_explanations.A: Discussing exceptions with management is part of the work, but the manager's agreement does not show where the 60 came from or let anyone repeat the test.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk assessment belongs in the engagement file and explains why the test exists. It does not record how the 60 claims were chosen.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a cross-reference is useful, and the work program states the planned sampling, but only the workpaper shows the population actually tested and how these 60 were drawn.

tips: Eliminate: A, because management's agreement on exceptions does not show how the claims were chosen, and C, because the risk assessment explains why the test exists, not how it was done.
Final two: B beats D because Standard 14.6 requires enough to repeat the work; the work program shows the plan, while the workpaper's population and selection let someone redo this test.
Exam cue: on CIA workpaper questions, apply the stranger test: could another competent auditor redo the work from the file alone and get the same result?

questions.subtopic: 2B8 Reaching engagement conclusions. Minor gaps that together weaken one control aim
questions.question: In an engagement on an airport's three fuel-loss controls, an internal auditor found a low-rated gap in each: late counts, unreconciled meter readings and unreviewed loss reports. On a two-level scale, which conclusion is best?

options.A: Satisfactory, since each finding on its own is rated low.
options.B: Unsatisfactory, as together the gaps weaken each loss check.
options.C: Satisfactory, with the gaps reported as one finding on losses.
options.D: Unsatisfactory, since three findings are too many to overlook.

questions.key_concept: The conclusion weighs findings together: minor gaps that weaken every control over one aim can add up to an unsatisfactory conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Look past each finding's own rating: what do the three gaps have in common, and what does that mean taken together?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.5 requires the conclusion to state the internal auditors' judgment of how significant the findings are taken together. Each gap looks minor alone, but all three loss controls are weakened at once, so none can make up for another, and on a two-level scale the processes cannot be called effective. Reporting one combined finding while concluding satisfactory, the closest choice, weighs the gaps in a finding but not in the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating each finding alone is the first step, not the conclusion. Standard 14.5 asks for the overall significance of the findings taken together.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: combining the gaps shows the right instinct, but a satisfactory verdict says the processes work while every loss check is weakened. The conclusion must carry the aggregate judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: The verdict follows the findings' combined significance, not their number. Three low findings on unrelated matters could still fit a satisfactory conclusion.

tips: Eliminate: A, because rating findings one by one is not weighing them together, and D, because the verdict follows combined significance, not the number of findings.
Final two: B beats C because Standard 14.5 puts the aggregate judgment in the conclusion itself; a combined finding beside a satisfactory verdict leaves the conclusion unweighed.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, weigh findings, do not count them: minor gaps that hit the same objective can add up to an unsatisfactory conclusion, and many unrelated ones need not.

questions.subtopic: 2B8 Reaching engagement conclusions. A conclusion that only lists findings
questions.question: An internal auditor drafts the conclusion for an assurance engagement on a chipmaker's payroll. The draft lists three rated findings with their root causes, and stops there. What does the draft conclusion most lack?

options.A: Management's action plans, with owners and due dates.
options.B: A statement that the work conformed with the Standards.
options.C: A judgment on how well the controls work, taken as a whole.
options.D: An overall rating equal to its highest-rated finding.

questions.key_concept: An assurance conclusion is the auditor's overall judgment on how effective governance, risk management and controls are; a list of findings is not a conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Which of these belongs in the conclusion itself, and which belongs elsewhere in the final communication?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.5, an assurance conclusion sums up the results against the engagement's objectives and management's, and says how effective the activity's governance, risk management and control processes are. A list of rated findings leaves that judgment unstated. Action plans with owners and dates, the closest choice, are required in the final communication under Standard 15.1, but they are not part of the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 15.1 requires owners and dates in the final communication, but they record management's response. The conclusion is the internal auditor's own overall judgment.
wrong_explanations.B: The final communication should carry a conformance statement when supervision and the quality program support it. It is not part of the conclusion, the auditor's overall judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: A methodology may give the conclusion a rating, but Standard 14.5 asks for judgment on the findings together and on the controls' effectiveness, not a copy of the worst rating.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a conformance statement belongs to the final communication, not the conclusion, and D, because copying the worst rating replaces the judgment the conclusion must state.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.5 makes the effectiveness judgment part of an assurance conclusion; owners and dates are final communication content under Standard 15.1.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a list of findings is not a conclusion. An assurance conclusion says how well the processes work, including when they work.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Technology tools for audit work. A checked model that flags nothing
questions.question: An internal auditor's model was validated on known duplicate claims. An insurer's 52,000 claims for the year in scope were reconciled to the ledger. The model checked all of them and flagged none. What is the auditor's best next step?

options.A: Conclude that the model's run found no duplicate payment.
options.B: Hand-test a random sample of claims to confirm the result.
options.C: Run the model on last year's claims too, before concluding.
options.D: Have the claims team run the model monthly as its own check.

questions.key_concept: Once a tool's logic is validated and its data reconciled, its full-population result is sufficient; rechecking a subset adds cost for little benefit.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool's result still lacks: were its logic and its data both checked? If so, what would more testing add?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 strengthens reliability when data is corroborated, and the ledger reconciliation did that; testing the model on known duplicates showed its logic works. Its run over the whole year lets another competent auditor repeat the work and reach the same result. Standard 4.2 weighs cost against benefit, so a hand sample, the closest choice, adds cost for little benefit, and Standard 14.2 then calls for assurance in the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a hand sample helps when a tool's logic or data is untested. Both were checked here, so a sample adds cost for little benefit (Standard 4.2).
wrong_explanations.C: The objective covers the year in scope. Last year's claims fall outside it, so running them adds work no objective asks for and delays the conclusion.
wrong_explanations.D: Handing management a monitoring routine is a possible later recommendation, not the step that completes this test. With a clean, reliable result, the next step is the conclusion (Standard 14.2).

tips: Eliminate: C, because last year's claims sit outside the year in scope, and D, because a monitoring routine for management is a later recommendation, not the step that completes this test.
Final two: A beats B because the model's logic and data were both checked; under Standard 4.2, a hand sample of the same records costs more than the little it adds.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, check a tool's logic and data before relying on it; once both pass, its full-population result can carry the conclusion without a manual backup.

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. Two exceptions in a sample of fifteen
questions.question: An internal auditor's approved program tests 15 of a university's grant payments over $20,000 for a second approver's sign-off. Two of the 15 lack the sign-off. What is the auditor's best next step?

options.A: Report the two as a finding, rated on the function's scale.
options.B: Test 45 more payments now, under the approved program as it stands.
options.C: Note the two as a potential finding, then start the next test.
options.D: Evaluate the two for cause, effect and any need for more tests.

questions.key_concept: A difference from criteria is a potential finding to evaluate; more testing follows only if due care calls for it, through an approved program change.
questions.pre_read: Two items differ from the criteria. Before reporting or testing more, what do the Standards ask the auditor to do with a difference?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 requires a difference between criteria and condition to be noted as a potential finding and then evaluated, and Standard 14.3 makes that evaluation the cause, effect and significance. Due care also decides whether the evidence needs more tests, which would go into an approved program change. Recording the two and moving on, the closest choice, notes the difference but leaves the evaluation undone.

wrong_explanations.A: Reporting comes after evaluation: Standard 14.3 asks for cause, effect and significance first, and two of fifteen payments do not yet show how far the gap reaches.
wrong_explanations.B: Under Standard 14.2, added testing needs an adjusted work program approved by the chief audit executive or a delegate; testing now under the unchanged program skips that step.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standard 14.2 requires the difference to be noted and then evaluated, including whether this test needs more evidence. Moving on leaves cause, effect and that decision unsettled.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a potential finding is evaluated for cause, effect and significance before it is reported, and B, because added testing needs an adjusted, approved work program.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 14.2 requires a difference to be noted and then evaluated; recording it and moving on stops at the first step.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a difference from criteria is noted, then evaluated; whether to test more is a due-care decision, and any added testing changes the program.

questions.subtopic: 2B7 Workpapers that support the results. A cause that rests on the manager's account
questions.question: An internal auditor traces a draft finding on a coffee depot's stock losses to the workpapers. The auditor checks the basis of each part. Which part most needs more support before review?

options.A: The rating, set on the function's scale, which the depot manager disputes.
options.B: The shortfall, from an independent stocktaker's count the auditor arranged.
options.C: The cause, a scanner fault since March, as the manager described it.
options.D: The loss, an estimate the auditor made with the depot's accountant.

questions.key_concept: Identifying a root cause with management does not make management's account evidence: the cause in a finding needs corroborating support in the workpapers.
questions.pre_read: For each part of the finding, ask where its support came from and whether another auditor could verify it from the file.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 requires the evidence behind engagement results to be documented, and Standard 4.3 calls for more evidence on statements that may be incomplete or false. A manager blaming losses on equipment is such a statement: working out root causes with management, as Standard 14.3 asks, does not make the manager's account the evidence. A disputed rating, the closest choice, rests on the function's scale; disagreement alone is not missing support.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a dispute calls for discussion, not more evidence by itself. Standard 13.1 does not oblige a change without a valid reason, and the rating follows the function's scale.
wrong_explanations.B: A count by an independent stocktaker the auditor arranged is information from an independent source, which Standard 14.1 says strengthens reliability, so the shortfall rests on solid support.
wrong_explanations.D: An estimated loss is normal: Standard 14.3 notes that exposure is often an estimate the auditor makes with input from the activity's management.

tips: Eliminate: B, because an independent stocktaker's count is a source Standard 14.1 treats as more reliable, and D, because a loss estimated by the auditor with the activity's input is expected practice.
Final two: C beats A because a manager's explanation of the cause is a claim that needs corroboration in the file, while a dispute over a rating is not missing evidence.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, trace each part of a finding to its evidence; a fact that rests only on the audited manager's account needs corroboration before the finding goes out.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. Testing a claim that complaints fell
questions.question: In an engagement on an online grocer's customer service, the manager says that complaints fell 30% this year and that this proves service improved. Which analysis best lets the internal auditor test the manager's claim?

options.A: Complaints per thousand orders, this year set against last year.
options.B: The number of complaints in each of the past five years.
options.C: This year's complaints against the target in the service plan.
options.D: The grocer's complaints per thousand orders against a rival's rate.

questions.key_concept: Pick the analysis that answers the objective: a raw count moves with volume, so a rate per unit of activity tests a quality claim.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else could make the complaint count fall, then pick the comparison that rules it out.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 requires information consistent with the objective, here whether this grocer's service improved this year. A raw count falls whenever orders fall, so complaints per thousand orders set against last year, a prior-period comparison Standard 14.2's considerations name, tests the claim. A rival's rate, the closest choice, shows how the grocer compares with another firm, not whether its own service changed.

wrong_explanations.B: A longer trend shows direction, but raw counts rise and fall with order volume, so five years of counts cannot separate better service from fewer orders.
wrong_explanations.C: A variance against target tests whether the plan was met. The target may itself ignore volume, and meeting it does not show whether service improved.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a rate per order fixes the volume problem, but a benchmark shows relative standing, not this year's change, and a rival may count complaints differently.

tips: Eliminate: B, because raw counts move with order volume however many years they cover, and C, because a variance against target answers whether the plan was met.
Final two: A beats D because the claim is about change this year, which a prior-period rate tests; a rival's rate shows relative standing, not change.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, pick the analytic that answers the objective; when a count can move with volume, compare a rate per unit of activity instead.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. Two supplier code sets before a duplicate test
questions.question: A merged wholesaler paid the same suppliers from two systems. Each system has only its own payments and supplier codes. Before testing extracts from both systems for duplicates, what should the internal auditor do first?

options.A: Remove records found in both extracts, so each payment counts once.
options.B: Map both systems' supplier codes to one common supplier list.
options.C: Test each system's extract on its own, as their supplier codes differ.
options.D: Ask each payments team for one merged file with the codes cleaned.

questions.key_concept: Normalizing makes records from different sources comparable; it never removes records, since repeated ones may be the very exceptions the test looks for.
questions.pre_read: Name the step between getting the data and analyzing it, then ask what that step must leave untouched.
questions.correct_explanation: A duplicate test across both systems needs one population with a common supplier key, so mapping the codes comes before analysis; the syllabus lists normalizing between obtaining data and analyzing it. Standard 14.1 requires sufficient information for the test, so no record is dropped: removing records found in both extracts, the closest choice, would delete the very payments the test exists to flag.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: removing records found in both extracts deletes the very payments a duplicate test should flag. Normalizing aligns formats and codes; it does not remove records.
wrong_explanations.C: Testing each file alone misses a supplier paid once from each system, the duplicate a merger makes likely. The files must be comparable before one test covers both.
wrong_explanations.D: A file merged and cleaned by the payments teams has passed through the hands of the activity under review, which weakens its reliability under Standard 14.1.

tips: Eliminate: C, because separate tests miss a supplier paid from both systems, and D, because a file cleaned by the audited teams is less reliable than the auditor's own extracts.
Final two: B beats A because the codes must be comparable before one test can cover both systems; removing records found in both would delete the duplicates being tested for.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about data analytics, normalize before you analyze: align codes, formats and units, and flag odd records rather than delete them.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. A reliable system record of every wire
questions.question: An internal auditor must learn whether wire transfers over $50,000 at a bank this year had a second approver. The treasury system logs both users, and tests found its controls effective. Which method is best?

options.A: Observe wire releases at unannounced times through the year.
options.B: Walk through one wire release with the treasury officer.
options.C: Review treasury's monthly reports of wires released by one person.
options.D: Extract the year's wire records and test those above the limit.

questions.key_concept: For whether a control operated every time over a period, a reliable system record of every instance beats watching some of them.
questions.pre_read: Ask which method covers the whole year, and what makes the records it would use trustworthy.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 asks for information that is relevant, reliable and sufficient. The objective covers the large wires for the whole year. Records the auditor extracts directly from a system with effective controls gain reliability on both counts, and testing all of them leaves nothing unseen, as the standard's considerations on complete populations support. Treasury's own reports, the closest choice, cover the year too, but the activity under review prepared them.

wrong_explanations.A: Watching releases is first-hand, but it covers only the moments seen. Where no record exists it is the best method; here the system logs every wire.
wrong_explanations.B: A walk-through of one release shows how the process is designed and how that wire went; it cannot show that every large wire this year had a second approver.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the reports cover the year, but treasury, the activity under review, prepared them; Standard 14.1 favors information obtained directly or from an independent source.

tips: Eliminate: A, because observation covers only the releases watched, not the whole year, and B, because one walk-through shows design and a single wire.
Final two: D beats C because both cover the year, but the auditor's own extract from a well-controlled system is stronger than reports the activity under review prepared.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, when two sources cover the same population, prefer the one the auditor obtains directly from a well-controlled system over the activity's own reports.

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. A corrected one-off loss against an open gap
questions.question: An internal auditor finds a $90,000 pricing error from a distributor's finished migration. The error was corrected and every price rechecked. The auditor also finds $4,000 of unapproved overrides that any clerk can still make. How should the auditor best prioritize the two findings?

options.A: The migration error, then the price overrides.
options.B: Both equal, as each caused a loss.
options.C: The overrides, then the migration error.
options.D: Neither, until management ranks them.

questions.key_concept: Significance weighs the likelihood and impact of the risk: a large loss whose cause is gone can matter less than a small, continuing gap.
questions.pre_read: For each finding, ask how likely it is to happen again and how far it could reach, not only what it has cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires significance to be judged by the likelihood of the risk and its impact, and findings ranked by it. The migration is finished, its error corrected and every price rechecked, so that risk is unlikely to recur. Any clerk can still override prices without approval, so that risk is likely, and its impact is not capped by the $4,000 found. Ranking by the larger past loss, the closest choice, confuses loss with risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the error cost more, but its cause is gone, so the risk is unlikely to recur. Significance weighs likelihood and impact, not past loss alone.
wrong_explanations.B: A loss in each case does not make two findings equal. Standard 14.3 weighs the likelihood and impact of each risk, and here they differ sharply.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal auditors evaluate significance and rank findings with the function's methodology; management's view is useful input but does not set the ranking.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a loss in each case does not make two risks equal, and D, because internal auditors rank findings, with management's view as input only.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.3 weighs the likelihood and impact of the risk; a corrected one-off error is unlikely to recur, while open overrides are not.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, rank findings by the risk they leave open, likelihood and impact together, not by the money already lost.

questions.subtopic: 2B7 Workpapers that support the results. A file from an engagement stopped midway
questions.question: An internal auditor's engagement at a depot ended midway because the depot was sold. Before that, the auditor's memo warned the depot manager of a gap. Policy keeps engagement files for six years. What should the auditor best do with the file?

options.A: Keep the whole partial file, memo included, for six years.
options.B: Keep the memo's evidence six years; dispose of the rest.
options.C: Dispose of the file once the depot's sale has closed.
options.D: Give the buyer a copy; keep the original six years.

questions.key_concept: Documentation is kept as law, regulation and policy require when work stops early too; retention covers the whole file, not just what was sent out.
questions.pre_read: Ask which rule sets how long the file is kept, and whether anything sent out during the work still needs its evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 has internal auditors keep engagement documentation for the periods that laws, regulations and the function's and organization's policies set, and policy here keeps engagement files six years. Stopping midway does not shrink the file: the unfinished work belongs to it, and so does the record of the memo that warned the manager. Keeping the memo's evidence and disposing of the rest, the closest choice, trims a file the policy covers.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the memo's evidence must stay, but so must the rest. The policy keeps the whole engagement file six years, unfinished work included (Standard 14.6).
wrong_explanations.C: The sale ends the work, not the duty to keep its file. Disposing of it before six years breaks the policy (Standard 14.6).
wrong_explanations.D: A copy is still a release. Records go to an outside party only as the function's release rules and confidentiality duties allow (Standard 5.2).

tips: Eliminate: C, because a sale ends the work but not the duty to keep its file, and D, because even a copy goes outside only by the approved release route.
Final two: A beats B because the policy covers the whole engagement file, unfinished work included; keeping only what supports the memo trims a file the policy protects (Standard 14.6).
Exam cue: on CIA questions, retention follows law, regulation and policy for the whole file, however the engagement ended; never trim a file down to the parts that were sent out.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. A second source when one record is weak
questions.question: An internal auditor queries a distributor's stock system. It shows every write-off as approved, but clerks type the approver's name. Approvals happen in a workflow tool, and IT keeps the tool's log. Which method best tests the approvals?

options.A: Have IT rerun the stock system query on a fresh extract.
options.B: Interview the approvers on how they use the workflow tool.
options.C: Observe the clerks as they record write-offs over the coming week.
options.D: Match each write-off to the workflow tool's recorded approvals.

questions.key_concept: Corroboration needs a second source for the same items; rerunning the same doubtful records, whoever runs them, adds no reliability.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the first result is in doubt, then which method draws on a different record of the same approvals.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 strengthens reliability when information is corroborated against more than one source. Here clerks type the approver's name, so the stock system cannot show who approved. The workflow log records approvals where they happen and is kept by IT, apart from the clerks, and matching every write-off covers the period. IT rerunning the query, the closest choice, reads the same field the clerks typed, so nothing is corroborated.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a fresh run by IT checks the query, not the data. The approver names still come from what clerks typed, so nothing is corroborated (Standard 14.1).
wrong_explanations.B: Approvers' accounts of how they use the tool explain the process; they cannot show that each write-off in the period was approved.
wrong_explanations.C: Observing next week's entries shows how clerks work now; it cannot show who approved the write-offs already recorded.

tips: Eliminate: B, because approvers' accounts describe the process but prove no single approval, and C, because next week's entries say nothing about write-offs already recorded.
Final two: D beats A because a second source corroborates; rerunning the query, even by IT, reads the same field the clerks typed (Standard 14.1).
Exam cue: on CIA questions, when a record is doubtful, corroborate it with a different source covering the same items; rerunning or reanalyzing the same data adds nothing.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. Choosing clinics to visit after a procedure change
questions.question: An internal auditor plans assurance on drug-stock controls at 40 clinics and must rank all 40 to choose which to visit. The stock procedure changed in March, after January's self-assessment survey. Which source is best?

options.A: The January self-assessment survey the 40 clinics completed.
options.B: A risk and control questionnaire sent to each clinic's manager.
options.C: The revised stock procedure the medical director approved in March.
options.D: Stock-count checklists completed at five clinics chosen at random.

questions.key_concept: To target site visits, use a current, low-cost source from every site; answers given before a process change describe the old process.
questions.pre_read: Ask what this step must decide, which sources reach every clinic, and which of those describe the process as it runs now.
questions.correct_explanation: Choosing clinics to visit needs current information on how each clinic runs its stock controls now. Standard 13.2 asks for reliable information when planning and for risks ranked for review, and Standard 14.1 counts information as reliable when it is current. A risk and control questionnaire to each manager gives that at low cost, to be tested at the clinics visited. The January survey, the closest choice, predates the March change.

wrong_explanations.C: Understanding the revised procedure is needed (Standard 13.2), but it is the same for all 40 clinics, so it cannot show which ones to visit.
wrong_explanations.D: Five clinics picked at random use no information on risk, so the visits may miss the clinics that most need them (Standard 13.2: rank risks for review).

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. A cause question and a request for a model
questions.question: An assurance engagement asks whether a courier company's new routing rule caused last quarter's rise in late deliveries. The operations head wants the internal auditor to model the best rule. Which analysis best fits?

options.A: Compare late-delivery rates by route before and after the rule.
options.B: Model which routing rule would cut late deliveries the most.
options.C: Forecast next quarter's late-delivery rate if the rule stays.
options.D: Flag single deliveries whose times fall far outside the usual range.

questions.key_concept: Pick the analysis that answers the engagement objective: a question about why something happened needs an analysis that explains it, whatever else is requested.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the objective's question is, a past cause, a future outcome or a best choice, and which analysis answers it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 treats information as relevant when it fits the engagement's objectives and scope. The objective asks why late deliveries rose, so the analysis needs to explain a past result: comparing each route's rates before and after the rule does that. A model recommending the best rule, the closest choice, answers the operations head's question, not the objective, and adding it would change the scope, which needs approval (Standard 13.3).

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a model of the best rule answers the operations head's request, not this objective; adding it changes the scope and needs approval first (Standard 13.3).
wrong_explanations.C: A forecast of next quarter's rate looks forward. The objective asks what caused last quarter's rise, which a forecast cannot explain.
wrong_explanations.D: Flags on single deliveries find odd cases to follow up; they do not test whether the rule drove the rise across all routes.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a forecast looks ahead while the objective asks about a past rise, and D, because flagging odd deliveries does not test the rule's effect.
Final two: A beats B because relevance comes from the engagement objective (Standard 14.1); the requested model answers a different question and would change the approved scope.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, match the analysis to the objective's question: why it happened, what may happen, or what to do. A stakeholder's request does not reset the objective.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. Which of four results to follow up
questions.question: An internal auditor's analytical review of a bus company tests whether costs and income fit what drives them. Those drivers are figures taken from records kept separately from finance. Which result most warrants follow-up work?

options.A: Stationery up 40%, with no driver found; under 1% of costs.
options.B: Payroll up 9%: 4% pay raise, flat headcount; 55% of costs.
options.C: Power up 12%: tariff up 8%, usage up 4%; 9% of costs.
options.D: Fare income down 15%: journeys down 15%, fares flat; 90% of income.

questions.key_concept: Follow-up goes where an unexplained difference is significant: weigh how much the drivers leave unexplained against how much the item matters.
questions.pre_read: For each result, find what its drivers leave unexplained, then ask how much that gap matters to the whole.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2's considerations relate financial figures to their drivers, such as payroll against employees, and weigh the significance of a difference and the cost of more analysis against its benefit before more work is done. Payroll's 9% rise leaves about 5 points unexplained on 55% of costs, the largest unexplained amount. Stationery, the closest choice, has the biggest unexplained percentage, but on under 1% of costs it matters far less.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the largest unexplained percentage, but on under 1% of costs a 40% rise is a small amount, and nothing here adds weight to it (Standard 14.2).
wrong_explanations.C: A tariff rise of 8% and usage up 4% together explain the 12% rise in power cost; nothing is left to follow up.
wrong_explanations.D: Journeys, counted apart from finance, fell 15% with fares flat, exactly as fare income did, so the income fits its drivers despite the large fall.

tips: Eliminate: C, because tariff and usage together explain the 12%, and D, because journeys counted apart from finance fell 15% with fares flat, as fare income did.
Final two: B beats A because follow-up weighs how much a gap matters, not its percentage alone: 5 unexplained points on 55% of costs outweigh 40% on under 1% (Standard 14.2).
Exam cue: on CIA questions, find the difference its drivers leave unexplained, then rank by how much it matters, not by the biggest percentage.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Technology tools for audit work. A dashboard built by the team under review
questions.question: An internal auditor tests an insurer's exception handling. The treasury team built a dashboard, fed from the payments system, that shows this year's payment exceptions were all cleared. What is the auditor's best next step?

options.A: Conclude from the dashboard's full-year view of every exception.
options.B: Observe treasury clearing exceptions on the dashboard for a week.
options.C: Test the feed's completeness and a sample of the cleared exceptions.
options.D: Have treasury certify in writing that the dashboard is complete.

questions.key_concept: A dashboard built by the team under review is not evidence until its feed's completeness and a sample of its results are tested.
questions.pre_read: Ask who built the tool, where its data comes from, and what would show that its picture is complete and true.
questions.correct_explanation: A dashboard summarizes data that someone else selected and processed, here the team under review. Standard 4.3 calls for a critical look at its reliability, and Standard 14.1 favors information obtained directly or corroborated. Testing that the feed brings in every exception, and that sampled clearances were real, shows whether its view can be used. Concluding from its full-year view, the closest choice, trusts a feed and flags that treasury set up.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a full-year view covers every exception only if its feed and clearing flags are right, and treasury set up both; untested, it is a lead (Standard 4.3).
wrong_explanations.B: A week of watching shows how treasury clears exceptions now; it cannot show that the year's exceptions all reached the dashboard or were truly cleared.
wrong_explanations.D: A written assurance from treasury is a claim by the team under review; it cannot replace testing the feed and the clearances.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a week of observation says nothing about the year's exceptions, and D, because treasury's certificate is the team's own claim, not evidence.
Final two: C beats A because full coverage is only as good as the feed and flags behind it; a tool the team under review built is tested before reliance (Standard 4.3).
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a tool built by the activity under review is a lead until its data and results are tested; full coverage alone does not make it reliable.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. Reliable replies that answer one part of the objective
questions.question: An internal auditor tests whether an insurer paid only named claimants with policies in force. Banks sent confirmations directly to the auditor. The confirmations give the account holder and policy reference for all 300 payments. Which is most accurate?

options.A: They support who was paid; policy cover needs other evidence.
options.B: They support both parts, as each reply names claimant and policy.
options.C: They support neither part, as banks keep no policy records.
options.D: They support who was paid once the claims team confirms each payment.

questions.key_concept: Evidence is weighed against each part of the objective: a reliable reply can carry a detail, such as a policy number, that it cannot prove.
questions.pre_read: Before judging how strong evidence is, ask which part of the engagement objective it actually speaks to.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.1, relevance is judged against the engagement objectives, apart from reliability. Replies the banks sent straight to the auditor are reliable and cover all 300 payments, so they support who was paid. The policy reference only repeats what the insurer wrote on each transfer, so the closest choice, reading it as proof of cover, fails: whether each policy was in force needs other evidence.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the banks are independent and every payment is covered, but a policy reference on a transfer shows what the insurer wrote, not that cover was in force.
wrong_explanations.C: The replies do bear on the first part: confirmations from independent banks are relevant to whether the named claimant was paid.
wrong_explanations.D: Replies sent straight to the auditor by independent banks already support who was paid; a confirmation from the claims team, part of the activity under review, adds little.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the replies are relevant to who was paid, and D, because independent replies sent straight to the auditor need no backing from the team under review.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 14.1 judges relevance against the objectives; a policy number on a transfer is reliable data about the payment, not proof of cover.
Exam cue: on CIA evidence questions, ask what a source can know. A reply can carry a detail, such as a reference number, that it is in no position to prove.

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. Last year's results in a repeat engagement
questions.question: Last year, an engagement found a port's crane-inspection control effective. An internal auditor is repeating the engagement for this year, and management says nothing has changed. Which view of last year's results is most accurate?

options.A: Updated for any change, they can serve as this year's condition.
options.B: They can shape this year's risk assessment, but not the condition.
options.C: They shape neither this year's risk assessment nor the condition.
options.D: Once management confirms no change, they serve as the condition.

questions.key_concept: An earlier engagement's results may shape planning, but the condition is determined from evidence gathered in the current engagement.
questions.pre_read: Ask which step a rule belongs to: what may be carried over into planning, and what must come from this engagement's own evidence?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 13.2, a repeat engagement builds on the earlier risk assessment by reviewing and updating it, so last year's results rightly shape planning. Standard 14.2, though, requires the condition to rest on evidence this engagement gathers, and last year's tests covered last year's inspections. Updating them for change, the closest choice, carries the planning rule into testing: the auditor still tests this year's inspections.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: review and update is Standard 13.2's rule for an earlier risk assessment; the condition must rest on evidence gathered in this engagement (Standard 14.2).
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 13.2 makes a review and update of the earlier engagement risk assessment the requirement, and its considerations list earlier communications and workpapers as sources, so the results shape planning.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's word that nothing changed is a statement to test, not evidence of the condition; Standard 4.3 calls for evidence behind what management says.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Standard 13.2 builds this year's risk assessment on the earlier one, and D, because management's word that nothing changed is a claim to test, not evidence of the condition.
Final two: B beats A because review and update is Standard 13.2's planning rule, while Standard 14.2 requires the condition to rest on evidence gathered in this engagement.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, ask which step a rule belongs to. A shortcut allowed in planning, such as updating an earlier risk assessment, does not carry into testing.

questions.question: An internal auditor is organizing a ferry firm's engagement file. The methodology allows clearing the 14 answered review notes and uses the file's dated sign-offs as evidence of review. Which step is most clearly required?

options.B: Cross-reference each workpaper to the work program step it completes.
options.C: Replace the sign-offs with the chief audit executive's approval of the file.
options.D: Keep each workpaper's review sign-off in the engagement file.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 14.6 says workpapers may follow the work program's structure and be cross-referenced; it helps a reviewer, but the Standards do not require it.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief audit executive must approve the documentation (Standard 14.6), but that approval adds to the evidence of supervision; it does not replace it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the methodology lets answered notes be cleared, and C, because the chief audit executive's approval of the file adds to, and never replaces, the record of supervision.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Technology tools for audit work. A validated model after its input data changed
questions.question: An internal auditor will target claims using an insurer's machine learning fraud model, validated in 2024. Claim forms have changed since then, and the model's owners say its code has not changed. What should the auditor do first?

options.A: Test its scores on recent claims whose outcomes are known.
options.B: Reperform the 2024 validation on the claims it was tested on.
options.C: Check its change log shows the code is the validated 2024 version.
options.D: Ask its owners to retrain it on claims made since the change.

questions.key_concept: A learning model's results depend on its data; when the data it sees has changed, revalidate it on current cases before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could make an unchanged model stop working: for ordinary software, a code change; for a learning model, a data change too.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST's AI framework warns that a model's results can drift when the data it now meets no longer matches the data it was built on, even with no code change. New claim forms are such a change, so the 2024 validation is not current evidence. Standard 14.1 needs reliable, current information, so the auditor first tests the scores on recent claims of known outcome. The closest choice, a change log, shows only unchanged code.

wrong_explanations.B: Rerunning the 2024 validation shows only how the model scored claims made before the forms changed. That is not current evidence that its scores still work (Standard 14.1).
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: unchanged code supports reliance on fixed-logic software. A learning model can drift when its data changes, so a code check cannot show its scores still work.
wrong_explanations.D: Retraining is the owners' decision and a possible later recommendation. A retrained model would still need testing before the auditor relies on it, so this does not come first.

tips: Eliminate: B, because rerunning the 2024 validation shows how the model worked before the forms changed, and D, because retraining is the owners' call and would still need testing.
Final two: A beats C because a learning model can drift when its data changes even if its code does not; Standard 14.1 needs current evidence that the scores still work.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, before relying on a model's output, the internal auditor usually asks whether its data has changed since it was validated, not only its code.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Technology tools for audit work. What an automated monitoring tool cannot judge
questions.question: An internal auditor has validated a bank's continuous monitoring tool, which flags dormant and privileged accounts daily. Each quarter, managers review whether each user's access fits the job. Which step best tests the managers' reviews?

options.A: Reperform the tool's daily checks on a sample of accounts.
options.B: Have the tool also flag access that does not fit each job.
options.C: Sample the tool's privileged-account flags and how each was resolved.
options.D: Inspect a sample of reviews and the access changes they triggered.

questions.key_concept: Automated monitoring covers checks that need little human judgment; a manager's review of whether access fits a job still needs its own test.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool can decide by itself and what still takes a person's judgment, then match the evidence to the control being tested.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST's continuous monitoring guide says automation suits checks needing little human involvement, and that not all monitoring can be automated. Whether a user's access fits the job is a manager's judgment this tool does not make. Standard 14.1 needs relevant evidence, so the auditor inspects a sample of reviews and the changes they triggered. Following up the tool's flags, the closest choice, tests the daily monitoring, not that judgment.

wrong_explanations.A: The auditor has already validated the tool. Rerunning its checks tests the dormant and privileged flags again, not whether managers judged each user's access against the job.
wrong_explanations.B: Changing the tool is management's design choice and a possible recommendation. It would not show whether managers' quarterly reviews, the control under test, actually operated.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: following up the tool's privileged-account flags tests the daily monitoring. Whether each user's access fits the job is a manager's judgment the tool does not make.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the tool is already validated and rerunning its checks does not test managers' reviews, and B, because changing management's tool is not a test of the reviews.
Final two: D beats C because automation covers checks needing little human judgment; following up the tool's flags tests the monitoring, not managers' judgment of fit (Standard 14.1).
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a validated tool's results support only the checks the tool itself performs; a control that rests on a person's judgment needs its own evidence.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. A To-Be map offered for this year's process
questions.question: An internal auditor is testing whether a port billed every vessel call this year. The auditor receives the billing manager's newly approved To-Be process map. Which use of the map is best?

options.A: As this year's process design, confirmed by walking calls through it.
options.B: As this year's criteria, testing billed calls against it.
options.C: As a planned change; map this year's process by walk-through.
options.D: As a planned change; assess whether the redesign will work.

questions.key_concept: A To-Be map shows a planned future process; the condition comes from how the process ran in the period, and criteria from rules in force.
questions.pre_read: Ask which state a process map shows, current or future, and which period the engagement tests, before using any map as condition or criteria.
questions.correct_explanation: An As-Is map records how a process works now; a To-Be map sets out the future state a redesign aims for (OpenStax, Foundations of Information Systems). So this map shows neither how billing ran this year nor the rules billing had to follow. The condition comes from evidence (Standard 14.2), so the auditor documents this year's process by walk-through before testing calls against bills. Confirming the map, the closest choice, would test the wrong design.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: walking items through a map suits an As-Is map of the current process. A To-Be map shows a planned future state, so it is not this year's design.
wrong_explanations.B: Criteria are chosen for the activity and period the scope sets (Standards 13.3 and 13.4). A design approved only now did not bind this year's billing.
wrong_explanations.D: Judging whether the redesign will work does not answer an objective about this year's billing (Standard 13.3), and this year's process would stay unmapped.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a design approved only now did not bind this year's billing, and D, because judging the redesign does not answer an objective about this year's billing.
Final two: C beats A because a To-Be map shows a planned future state, not how billing ran this year; this year's process comes from walking real calls through it (Standard 14.2).
Exam cue: on CIA questions, check what a document describes, current or planned, and which period it covers before using it as the condition or the criteria.
