questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. Two measures on different scales before a ranking
questions.question: An internal auditor will rank 50 fuel stations for visits by adding each station's cash shortages, in dollars, to its count of voided sales. Which handling of the data best suits the ranking?

options.A: Rescale both measures to a common range before adding them.
options.B: Remove stations with extreme values before adding the measures.
options.C: Divide each station's combined total by its sales before ranking.
options.D: Add the raw figures, then judge whether the ranking looks right.

questions.key_concept: Before combining measures kept in different units, put them on a common scale, so no measure swamps the others just because its numbers are bigger.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the data is ready for the analysis: are the measures being combined on the same scale, or will one drown out the other?
questions.correct_explanation: Data preparation comes before analysis, and normalizing rescales measures to a common range, so a measure recorded in large numbers cannot outweigh the others by size alone (OpenStax, Foundations of Information Systems). Dollar shortages would swamp a count of voids, so the auditor rescales both first, letting each measure count in the ranking (Standard 14.1). Dividing by sales, the closest choice, adjusts for station size but still mixes dollars and counts.

wrong_explanations.B: Extreme stations may be the riskiest ones the ranking exists to find. Treating outliers can suit other analyses, but dropping them here defeats the objective (Standard 14.1).
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: dividing by sales adjusts for each station's size, but the total still mixes dollars and counts, so shortages still swamp the voids.
wrong_explanations.D: Judging the result by eye after adding raw figures skips data preparation. The ranking would mostly follow the dollar column, and a look would not show why.

tips: Eliminate: B, because extreme stations may be the very ones to visit, and D, because adding raw figures before preparing the data analyzes first and checks later.
Final two: A beats C because measures in different units need a common scale before they are added; dividing the mixed total by sales adjusts for station size, not for units.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, prepare data before analyzing it: integrate, clean and put measures on a common scale, without deleting the odd records that may be exceptions.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. An advisory request to recommend one of three options
questions.question: In an advisory engagement, a water utility's management asks an internal auditor to recommend one of three meter-reading schedules to cut estimated bills. Which analysis best fits?

options.A: Find what drove last year's estimated bills in each billing area.
options.B: Summarize last year's estimated bills by area and meter type.
options.C: Pilot the three schedules in one area each, then adopt the best.
options.D: Simulate estimated bills under each schedule, and rank the three.

questions.key_concept: When the agreed objective asks which action works best, prescriptive analysis fits; in advisory work the auditor recommends and management decides.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the agreed objective asks for (what happened, why, what next or what to do) and who makes the final choice.
questions.correct_explanation: Prescriptive analytics compares possible actions, often by simulating each one, to recommend the best; diagnostic analytics looks for the causes of past results (OpenStax, Foundations of Information Systems). The agreed objective asks which schedule to recommend, so the auditor simulates all three and ranks them, leaving the choice to management, as advisory services take on no management responsibility (Glossary). Finding last year's causes, the closest choice, compares no schedules.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: finding causes is diagnostic work and may inform the options. The objective asks which of three schedules to recommend, which needs the three compared.
wrong_explanations.B: A summary of last year's bills describes what happened. It cannot show which schedule would cut estimated bills the most.
wrong_explanations.C: Adopting a schedule is management's decision; advisory services give advice without taking on management responsibilities (Glossary). Running live pilots also goes beyond the agreed objective.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a summary of last year shows what happened, not what to do, and C, because adopting a schedule is management's decision, not internal audit's.
Final two: D beats A because prescriptive analysis compares actions to recommend one, while diagnostic analysis explains a past result; the agreed objective asks for a recommendation.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, match the method to the objective's question: what happened, why, what next, or what to do. Whatever the method, management makes the decision.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. A steady current ratio and a falling quick ratio
questions.question: An internal auditor is reviewing a wholesaler's working capital. The current ratio was steady at 2.0 for two years, while the quick ratio fell from 1.1 to 0.5. Which view best directs the follow-up?

options.A: Liquidity held, as the current ratio shows; no follow-up is needed.
options.B: Inventory or prepaid costs now form more of current assets; test why.
options.C: Customers pay more slowly; test receivables aging and credit terms.
options.D: Liquid assets no longer cover short-term debts; report a finding.

questions.key_concept: The quick ratio leaves inventory and prepaid costs out of current assets, so a falling quick ratio beside a steady current ratio points to them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each ratio includes, and what must have changed for one to fall while the other holds steady.
questions.correct_explanation: The current ratio sets all current assets against current liabilities; the quick ratio leaves out inventory and prepaid costs, which take longer to turn into cash (OpenStax, Principles of Accounting, Appendix A). One steady and the other falling means those items now make up more of current assets. The auditor tests why stock or prepayments built up, analyzing further before any finding (Standard 14.2). Receivables, the closest choice, count in both ratios.

wrong_explanations.A: A steady current ratio does not show a shift inside current assets. The falling quick ratio shows more of them are now slow to turn into cash.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: receivables are quick assets, counted in both ratios. Slower collection alone would not lower the quick ratio while the current ratio held steady.
wrong_explanations.D: True, quick assets now cover only half of short-term debts, but no criteria breach is shown. A ratio's move is a lead for more analysis, not a finding (Standard 14.2).

tips: Eliminate: A, because a steady current ratio does not show a shift inside current assets, and D, because a ratio's move is a lead for more analysis, not yet a finding.
Final two: B beats C because the quick ratio leaves out only inventory and prepaid costs; receivables sit in both ratios, so slower collection cannot explain the gap.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, read related ratios together: when they move apart, ask what one includes that the other leaves out, then follow up that item.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. A falling receivables turnover and a growth explanation
questions.question: An internal auditor reviews a printing firm's credit control. Sales increased 5%, and receivables turnover fell from 9 to 5 times. The credit manager says sales growth explains the fall. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Growth may explain it; confirm the 5% rise in the sales ledger.
options.B: Customers now pay faster, so less cash is tied up.
options.C: Receivables grew far faster than sales; the cause needs testing.
options.D: Unsold stock built up; count inventory against the sales records.

questions.key_concept: Receivables turnover sets sales against average receivables, so sales growth alone does not lower it; a sharp fall means receivables outgrew sales.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the ratio compares, and whether the explanation offered would move it that far in that direction.
questions.correct_explanation: Receivables turnover sets credit sales against average receivables, and a lower figure means cash comes in more slowly relative to sales (OpenStax, Principles of Accounting, Appendix A). Sales up 5% cannot take it from 9 to 5: receivables must have grown far faster than sales. Under Standard 4.3, the auditor seeks evidence of the cause before any finding (Standard 14.2). Confirming the sales rise, the closest choice, tests a fact that cannot explain the fall.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: confirming the 5% rise checks a fact, not the explanation. Turnover already divides sales by receivables, so 5% growth cannot take it from 9 to 5 (Standard 4.3).
wrong_explanations.B: A lower turnover means receivables are collected fewer times a year, so cash comes in more slowly, not faster.
wrong_explanations.D: Receivables turnover sets credit sales against receivables; stock plays no part in it. A build-up of unsold stock would show in inventory turnover instead.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a lower turnover means slower collection, not faster, and D, because unsold stock plays no part in receivables turnover.
Final two: C beats A because turnover already sets sales against receivables, so even a confirmed 5% rise cannot take it from 9 to 5; the explanation itself fails (Standard 4.3).
Exam cue: on CIA questions, test a manager's explanation against what the ratio compares: an explanation that would not move the ratio that far needs corroboration.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. A spending trend against a common-size share
questions.question: An engagement objective asks whether a bus company's depot has kept spending more on maintenance each year since repairs were outsourced in 2022. Which analysis best answers it for the internal auditor?

options.A: Maintenance costs in 2026 against 2022, as a dollar and percent change.
options.B: Maintenance costs from 2022 through 2026, with 2022 as the base year.
options.C: Maintenance as a percentage of total depot costs, 2022 through 2026.
options.D: Maintenance costs in 2026 against the 2026 budget, line by line.

questions.key_concept: Match the technique to the objective: a trend over several periods follows an amount over time; common-size figures follow its share of a total.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the objective is about an amount, its share of a total or a plan, and over how many periods.
questions.correct_explanation: Horizontal (trend) analysis sets a line item for each period against a base year and is most useful over several periods, since a trend is hard to see without them (OpenStax, Principles of Accounting, Appendix A). Costs for every year since 2022 show whether spending rose each year (Standard 14.1). Maintenance as a percentage of total costs, the closest choice, is vertical (common-size) analysis: it tracks a share, which can fall while spending rises.

wrong_explanations.A: Two years give one change, not the path between them: spending could have fallen in 2024 and recovered by 2026. A trend needs the years in between.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: common-size analysis shows maintenance as a share of total costs. If other costs grew faster, that share would fall even while maintenance spending rose every year.
wrong_explanations.D: A budget variance tests whether one year's spending met its plan. It shows nothing about the direction of spending since 2022, and budgets can rise too.

tips: Eliminate: A, because two years give one change, not the path between them, and D, because one year's budget variance tests the plan, not the direction of spending.

Final two: B beats C because the objective concerns the amount spent over time, which horizontal analysis follows; common-size analysis follows a share of total costs, which can fall while spending rises.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, match the technique to the question: change over time calls for a trend across several periods; the make-up of a total calls for common-size figures.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. A tagged event log whose elements vary by type
questions.question: An internal auditor gets an online retailer's event log to test whether each refund over $500 had a second approver. The log uses tags to label each event's elements, which vary by type. Which handling best fits?

options.A: Query the log's elements directly, as the ledger's tables are queried.
options.B: Export the log as text, then search for refunds naming no approver.
options.C: Parse each event's elements into fields, then select the refunds.
options.D: Run anomaly detection on the log for unusually large refunds.

questions.key_concept: Tagged records whose elements vary are semistructured data: parse the tags into fields before testing, as the records do not fit a fixed table.
questions.pre_read: Ask what shape the data has, fixed rows and columns, tagged elements or free text, and what each shape needs.
questions.correct_explanation: Tags that label elements varying by event type mark semistructured data: partly organized, yet not a neat table, and parsers read it (OpenStax, Foundations of Information Systems, Section 3.1). Parsing puts each event's amount and approver into fields, so the auditor can test every refund over $500 (Standard 14.1). Querying it like the ledger's tables, the closest choice, treats it as structured data held in fixed rows and columns, which these events lack.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: table queries suit structured data in fixed rows and columns. These events carry different elements by type, so they do not fit the ledger's tables until parsed.
wrong_explanations.B: Text search suits unstructured data such as contracts. Treating the log as text ignores the tags that mark each element, and a word search cannot compare amounts with $500.
wrong_explanations.D: Anomaly detection flags what stands out, such as unusual amounts, but the objective is whether each refund over $500 had a second approver, which a flag cannot show.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a word search reads tagged data as free text and cannot compare amounts with $500, and D, because flagging unusual amounts shows nothing about second approvers.
Final two: C beats A because tags marking elements that vary by event type make the log semistructured; it is parsed into fields before it can be queried like a table.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, name the data type before the method: fixed tables suit direct queries, tagged records are parsed before table tools work, and free text is searched.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. An interview claim the approval log cannot rule out
questions.question: An internal auditor is testing approvals at a dairy. A clerk says that, on the clerk's days off, the finance manager uses the clerk's login. The approval log shows only authorized users. How should the auditor best treat the clerk's statement?

options.A: As grounds to test that login's approvals against leave records.
options.B: As outweighed by the log, a record of every approval's user.
options.C: As outside the objective, which covers approvals rather than logins.
options.D: As grounds to have IT disable the clerk's login at once.

questions.key_concept: An interview can surface facts a record cannot show, such as who really used a login; a conflicting claim is grounds to change the tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each piece of evidence actually records, and whether it could prove a person's claim wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Inquiry can bring out information that conflicts with other evidence, such as possible management override, and justify changing the tests (ISA 500, paragraphs A26 to A29). The log shows the login, not who used it, so it cannot rule the claim out; under Standard 14.1 the auditor decides whether more information is needed, and leave records kept outside finance can test it. The closest choice lets the log outweigh a claim it cannot test.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: documents usually outweigh oral evidence, but only on what they record. The log names the login used, not the person using it, so it cannot disprove the clerk.
wrong_explanations.C: Who really approved each payment is the core of an approval test, so a claim that another person used the clerk's login bears directly on the objective.
wrong_explanations.D: Disabling access is a control change for management to decide, not the auditor, and it would not show who approved the payments.

tips: Eliminate: C, because who really approved is the core of an approval test, and D, because changing access is management's decision, and it would not show who approved the payments.
Final two: A beats B because the log records which login approved, not who used it, so it cannot disprove the clerk; a claim it cannot test is grounds for a test that can.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, an interview claim that conflicts with a record calls for more work; first ask whether the record could actually show the claim false.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. Clean results on the riskiest payments, then a conclusion on all
questions.question: An internal auditor tests approval of an airline's 2,800 supplier payments. The auditor checked all 120 made to new suppliers, the riskiest group. All were approved. Which step best supports a conclusion on all 2,800?

options.A: Conclude on the 2,800, as the riskiest payments all passed.
options.B: Recalculate each of the 120 payments against its supplier invoice.
options.C: Test a sample drawn from across the other 2,680 payments.
options.D: Test every payment over $250,000 among the other 2,680.

questions.key_concept: Items chosen because they look riskiest are not a sample: clean results on them say nothing about the lower-risk rest of the population.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the tested items were chosen, and whether that choice lets them stand for the rest of the population.
questions.correct_explanation: Payments chosen because they carry the most risk are specific items, not a sample, so their results cannot be projected to the rest (ISA 500, paragraphs A65 and A66). Clean results on the riskiest 120 do not show the other 2,680 were approved. Standard 14.1 requires sufficient evidence, and a sample should represent its population, so the 2,680 need a sample. Concluding now, the closest choice, reads risk-based clean results as covering the rest.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: testing the riskiest payments first is sound, but they are specific items; their passing says nothing about whether the lower-risk 2,680 were approved.
wrong_explanations.B: Recalculation checks arithmetic, which bears on accuracy, not approval, and it adds nothing about the 2,680 payments the conclusion must also cover.
wrong_explanations.D: Payments over an amount are also specific items, chosen for size; like the 120, their results cannot be projected to the remaining payments.

tips: Eliminate: B, because recalculating checks arithmetic, not approval, and covers only the 120, and D, because items chosen by size are specific items whose results cannot be projected either.
Final two: C beats A because clean results on the riskiest items are not evidence about the rest; only a sample drawn from the 2,680 can be projected to them.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, items picked because they look risky are a targeted test, not a sample; however clean, their results speak only for the items tested.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. A difference inside the limit at a high-risk shop
questions.question: An internal auditor's approved program accepts sales within 5% of expectation across a bakery chain's 20 shops. The limit was set for normal-risk shops. Shop 7 has high fraud risk, and its sales are 4% below expectation. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: A potential finding, as sales fell short of the expectation.
options.B: Worth following up, as a riskier shop warrants a tighter limit.
options.C: Acceptable, as it falls inside the program's approved limit.
options.D: Worth following up only if the chain's total falls short too.

questions.key_concept: The difference accepted without follow-up should shrink as risk rises, so a result inside a single limit can still need follow-up where risk is high.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether one limit set for every unit fits a unit whose assessed risk is higher than the rest.
questions.correct_explanation: The difference an auditor accepts without investigating shrinks as assessed risk rises (ISA 520, paragraphs 5(d) and A16), so one 5% limit for all 20 shops is too wide for Shop 7. Standard 14.2 has the auditor use due care, weighing the engagement risk assessment, to decide whether more analysis is needed; the adjusted program needs the chief audit executive's approval. Accepting the result because the limit allows it, the closest choice, ignores that risk.

wrong_explanations.A: An expectation is the auditor's estimate, not criteria; a shortfall against it is a lead, and only follow-up showing a gap against criteria makes a potential finding.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the approved limit is the starting rule, but one limit for every shop ignores Shop 7's higher risk; a riskier unit warrants a smaller accepted difference.
wrong_explanations.D: A shop's shortfall can vanish inside the chain's total; Shop 7's own risk rating, not the chain's result, decides whether its 4% needs follow-up.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a shortfall against an expectation is a lead, not yet a gap against criteria, and D, because a shop's shortfall can vanish in the chain's total; Shop 7's own risk decides.
Final two: B beats C because the difference accepted without investigation shrinks as risk rises; a limit set for all 20 shops is too wide for the one rated high.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a result inside a limit is not automatically fine; ask whether that unit's risk justifies the same limit as the rest.
